content: The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) strategy was developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to address the high mortality and morbidity rates among children under five years of age in lowand middle-income countries. This strategy aims to improve the quality of care and reduce child deaths by implementing a combination of curative and preventive interventions at health facilities, in homes, and within communities. To evaluate the effectiveness of the IMCI strategy, researchers conducted a systematic review of studies, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled before-after (CBA) studies. These studies assessed the impact of IMCI on child mortality, nutritional status, quality of care, coverage of health interventions, and satisfaction of beneficiaries. The review included data from two cluster-randomized trials (conducted in India and Bangladesh) and two CBA studies (conducted in Tanzania and India). The interventions studied included training healthcare workers, strengthening health systems, and conducting home visits. Some studies also focused on neonatal care packages. One trial in Bangladesh suggested that IMCI might reduce child mortality by 13%, but the confidence interval (CI) included the possibility of no effect (risk ratio [RR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.10; low-certainty evidence). Similarly, a CBA study in Tanzania reported nearly identical results (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.05). In India, a trial implementing the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) strategy, which included postnatal home visits, found that neonatal and infant mortality might be lower in the IMNCI group compared to the control group (infant mortality hazard ratio [HR] 0.85, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.94; neonatal mortality HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.03; low-certainty evidence). When combining data from the IMCI and IMNCI trials, the analysis suggested that IMCI might reduce overall mortality (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.93; low-certainty evidence). Regarding nutritional status, two trials (India and Bangladesh) indicated that IMCI might have little or no effect on stunting (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.06; low-certainty evidence) and probably has little or no effect on wasting (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.25; moderate-certainty evidence). Similar findings were observed in the Tanzania CBA study. The quality of care was assessed by observing prescribing practices for common illnesses at health facilities and by lay healthcare workers. However, the evidence was of very low certainty, and no consistent effects on prescribing practices were identified. For coverage of IMCI deliverables, such as vaccine and vitamin A coverage, appropriate care-seeking behavior, and exclusive breastfeeding, the results were mixed. Two trials (India and Bangladesh) found that IMCI probably has little or no effect on measles vaccine coverage (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.05; moderate-certainty evidence), with similar findings in the Tanzania CBA study. There was little or no evidence of increased coverage for the third dose of the diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus vaccine or for vitamin A supplementation. Four studies (two from India, one from Tanzania, and one from Bangladesh) assessed maternal care-seeking behavior. While some studies suggested improved care-seeking behavior, others did not, resulting in mixed findings. Similarly, the impact of IMCI on exclusive breastfeeding was unclear, with very low-certainty evidence and inconsistent results. No studies reported on the satisfaction of mothers or service users. In conclusion, the IMCI strategy may reduce child mortality, and interventions targeting the neonatal period may reduce infant mortality. However, IMCI appears to have little or no effect on nutritional status and vaccine coverage. The evidence regarding maternal care-seeking behavior and exclusive breastfeeding is mixed and of very low certainty. Further research is needed to better understand the impact of IMCI on these outcomes.
